rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains mountain uplift as part of the crust's gradual balancing during cooling and hardening; pressure from overlying material, especially mountains, supports a partly solid interior.
rows.anchor: the mountains owe their rise to the gradual balancing process to which the solid crust of the earth is subject

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says this relative, quake-and-volcano-disrupted equilibrium makes life possible; “lest it sway with you” refers to the solid crust against an unstable interior, with mountains as the “pegs” of 78:7.
rows.anchor: it is the solidity of the earth's crust - as contrasted with its possibly fluid but certainly very unstable interior - which makes life on earth possible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that ummah may mean a period of time, yielding the alternative rendering “at every period.”
rows.anchor: Or "at every period", since the term ummah has this significance as well.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a wider sense, Asad allows ummah to mean a civilization, encompassing both a human group and a period of time.
rows.anchor: In its wider sense, it may also be taken here to denote "civilization", thus comprising a human groupment as well as a period of time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur'anic worship of God entails human responsibility; this concise command sums up ethical duties and prohibitions, grounds all morality, and conveys the unchanging message of every true religion.
rows.anchor: the above commandment comprises, in the most concise formulation imaginable, the sum-total of all ethical injunctions and prohibitions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those whom God guided are the people who availed themselves of guidance He offered to all human beings.
rows.anchor: who availed themselves of the guidance offered by Him to all human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase literally as error having inevitably become established against someone, or a verdict of error becoming inevitable for them.
rows.anchor: upon whom error came to be inevitably established (haqqa 'alayhi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The person in question is one whose heart God seals because of persistent, conscious refusal to submit to His guidance.
rows.anchor: one whose heart "God has sealed" in consequence of his persistent, conscious refusal to submit to His guidance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad notes that the passive wording literally means “he was called.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "he was called".

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators take tuwan or tuwa as the proper name of the hallowed valley.
rows.anchor: the word tuwan (or tuwa) is the name of the "hallowed valley"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Asad prefers Zamakhshari's reading of tuwan or tuwa as “twice,” making the valley twice hallowed because God's voice was heard there and Moses was raised there to prophethood.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari explains it, more convincingly, as meaning "twice" (from tuwan or Owan, "twice done")

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad identifies Pharaoh's claim to divine status as his greatest sin.
rows.anchor: Pharaoh's greatest sin, namely, his claim to divine status

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the tentative clause as the messenger's intention or hope of prompting Pharaoh, not uncertainty in God's knowledge of his future response.
rows.anchor: it relates to the intention or hope with which the message-bearer should approach his task (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Qur'anic narratives convey enduring truths about human behavior, Asad says the command to speak gently remains valid for all times and every effort at conversion.
rows.anchor: to speak to one particular sinner "in a mild manner, so that he might (have a chance to] bethink himself" retains its validity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers fear Pharaoh might banish or kill them outright, preventing them from fully delivering God's message.
rows.anchor: lest he prevent us, by banishing or killing us outright, from delivering Thy message fully

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to Qur'anic parallels and Exodus i, 8–22 for a fuller description of Pharaoh's oppression of the Israelites.
rows.anchor: For a more detailed description of this Pharaonic oppression of the Israelites, see Exodus i, 8-22.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari, Razi and Baydawi
rows.claim: Zamakhshari, Razi, and Baydawi read araynahu here as “made him acquainted with” or “made him aware of,” although its literal sense is “We showed him.”
rows.anchor: According to Zamakhshari, Razi and Baydawi, this verb has here the meaning of "We made him acquainted with" or "aware of".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The signs shown to Pharaoh include both the messages entrusted to Moses and the intangible messages conveyed by God's creation in the preceding passage.
rows.anchor: both those entrusted directly to Moses and the intangible "messages" forthcoming from God's creation

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains “wherever he may come” to mean that a sorcerer cannot succeed whether pursuing a good or an evil end.
rows.anchor: "wherever he may come" - i.e., irrespective of whether he aims at a good or at an evil end (Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the statement as a categorical condemnation of every practice of magic, regardless of the practitioner's intention.
rows.anchor: The above statement implies a categorical condemnation of all endeavours which fall under the heading of "magic"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 7:117–119 for the parallel account of the sorcerers' defeat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to note 90 on 7:120 for the parallel account of the sorcerers' response.
rows.anchor: See note 90 on 7:120.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The “him” in Pharaoh's accusation refers to Moses.
rows.anchor: I.e., Moses (cf. note 91 on 7:123).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Pharaoh's verb forms convey the stress on carrying out the mutilations and crucifixions in great numbers.
rows.anchor: Regarding the meaning of the stress on "great numbers", forthcoming from the grammatical form of the verbs employed by Pharaoh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied comparison is between Pharaoh and the God in whom the magicians now believe.
rows.anchor: Sc., "I or the God in whom you now believe".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to his note on 7:150 for the parallel account of Aaron's response.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the phrase as “my word” or “what I had said.”
rows.anchor: "to my word" or "to what I had said"

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari takes Aaron's prior instruction to concern the importance of keeping the Israelites united.
rows.anchor: evidently, about the importance of keeping the people united (Zamakhshari)

rows.speaker: most of the commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take azwajan minhum to refer to the deniers of truth discussed in the preceding passages.
rows.anchor: According to most of the commentators, this relates to the deniers of the truth spoken of in the preceding passages

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad broadens the phrase to mean “so many others,” reading the injunction as a general condemnation of envy rather than one limited to truth-deniers.
rows.anchor: since the above injunction has obviously a wider purport, condemning envy in general, I have rendered this expression as "so many others"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says what God grants a person reflects divine wisdom and is appropriate to that person's decreed destiny.
rows.anchor: whatever God grants a person is an outcome of divine wisdom and, therefore, truly appropriate to the destiny which God has decreed for that person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, Asad says the phrase may refer to the hereafter and the spiritual sustenance God gives the righteous.
rows.anchor: Alternatively, the phrase may be understood as referring to the life to come and the spiritual sustenance which God bestows upon the righteous.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the sentence as saying prayer benefits people alone, since God is exalted above any need of benefits; Asad's “for Us” interpolation follows this reading.
rows.anchor: Razi's interpretation of the above sentence: "God makes it clear that He has enjoined this [i.e., prayer] upon men for their own benefit alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says prayer is a spiritual benefit for the worshipper, not a tribute owed to a jealous God, a portrayal he associates with the Old Testament in its present corrupted form.
rows.anchor: prayer must not be conceived as a kind of tribute to a "jealous God"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses taqwa as “God-consciousness.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "to God-consciousness".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's literal rendering is “and yet in their heedlessness they are obstinate.”
rows.anchor: Lit., "and yet in [their] heedlessness they are obstinate (mu'ridun)"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says God is utterly remote from the imperfection implied by the idea of offspring.
rows.anchor: utterly remote from the imperfection implied in the concept of "offspring"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged divine offspring allude to prophets such as Jesus, called God's son by Christians, and angels whom pre-Islamic Arabs imagined as female daughters of God.
rows.anchor: This alludes to prophets like Jesus, whom the Christians regard as "the son of God", as well as to the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the deniers' admission of heedlessness as deliberate and inexcusable because prophets had warned humanity of resurrection and judgment.
rows.anchor: deliberately and without any excuse, since all the prophets had warned man of the Day of Resurrection and Judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad's added phrase “bent on” marks intent in “those who deny the truth,” paralleling his interpretation of alladhina kafaru in 2:6.
rows.anchor: The words "bent on" interpolated by me within brackets indicate intent, similar to the preceding expression alladhina kafaru

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah interpret the two phrases as the various stages of embryonic development; Asad says his “complete yet incomplete” rendering conforms to their view.
rows.anchor: mukhallaqah wa-ghayr mukhallaqah by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah

rows.speaker: Tabari
rows.claim: Tabari explains ghayr mukhallaqah as the mudghah stage before individual life, when no soul has yet been breathed into it.
rows.anchor: Tabari explains the expression ghayr mukhallaqah as denoting the stage at which the embryonic lump (mudghah) has as yet no individual life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation from dust indicates humanity's lowly biological origin and affinity with other earthy substances.
rows.anchor: man's lowly biological origin and his affinity with other "earthy" substances

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his note on 16:70 for the parallel discussion of declining knowledge in old age.
rows.anchor: See note 79 on 16:70.
